title: Judge Vacates Four-Year Visa Cap, Restoring Duration of Status for Students
excerpt: A Massachusetts federal judge set aside the DHS rule in full, holding it arbitrary and beyond the agency's authority — F-1, J-1 and I visa holders keep the status framework they have used for decades.
body:
• A federal judge in Massachusetts on Monday vacated the Department of Homeland Security rule that would have capped F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors at four years in the United States, restoring the longstanding duration-of-status system in full.
  • Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV held that the rule was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act and that its restrictions on academic study exceeded DHS's statutory authority.
  • Nothing changes for current students: there is no extension application to file and no four-year deadline to track. Duration of status remains in effect nationwide while the administration decides whether to appeal.
  • The ruling lands the same day Open Doors reported Indian enrolment in the US fell in 2025-26, with Indian graduate numbers down about a third.

International students in the United States will not face a four-year clock on their studies. US District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV on Monday set aside the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulation that would have ended "duration of status" — the framework that has for decades let F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors remain in the country while they make progress toward a degree or programme — and replaced it with fixed admission periods of no more than four years, according to Bloomberg Law.

Who is affected — and who is not

The vacated rule covered three groups: F-1 international students, J-1 exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media on I visas, for whom it would have set a 240-day admission limit. Under the rule, a student whose programme ran past four years — a common position for doctoral candidates, whose research often takes five to seven years — would have had to apply to the government for an extension of stay, and the rule would also have restricted students' ability to change educational objectives, transfer institutions, or pursue additional programmes of study. No other visa categories were touched by the rule, and none are touched by Monday's ruling: what changes is only that the new restrictions will not take effect.

What the court held

Saylor granted summary judgment to the coalition that sued — NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, the American Federation of Teachers, two teachers' and auto workers' union bodies, and The NewsGuild-CWA — and denied the government's motion. In its statement on the ruling, the coalition said the court held the rule arbitrary and capricious because DHS failed to weigh its costs and benefits appropriately, justify the changes on its stated fraud and national-security grounds, consider less burdensome alternatives, or respond adequately to significant public comments. The court pointed to one alternative in particular: improving the existing Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), rather than imposing a costly new system.

"The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program."

— Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, US District Court for the District of Massachusetts

On the fraud rationale, Bloomberg Law reported, Saylor wrote that the agency had not explained how "an unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system — after a foreign student has already been in the country for four years — meaningfully enhances the ability of DHS to root out cases of fraud," or how its benefits would outweigh the costs of abandoning the existing system. The case is Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 1:26-cv-13799, in the District of Massachusetts, filed on August 18, 2026. Saylor had already stopped the regulations from taking effect in September, a day before their scheduled start; Monday's order converts that pause into a final judgment against the rule itself.

What to do next

For students and exchange visitors, the answer is: nothing new. Duration of status remains the governing framework nationwide, so a student in good standing who is progressing toward their programme's completion does not need to file an extension application keyed to a four-year anniversary, and planned transfers or changes of programme are governed by the rules that applied before the DHS regulation was finalised on July 17, 2026. The administration is expected to appeal, but an appeal by itself does not reinstate the rule; unless a higher court revives it, the four-year cap stays off the books. Students with individual complications — a change of status, a reinstatement, a programme extension through their school — should still work through their campus designated school official, as before.

Why the ruling matters for Indian students

India is the largest source of international students in the United States, and the ruling arrived on the same day as new Open Doors figures showing that pipeline shrinking. As we reported earlier today, Indian enrolment fell in the 2025-26 year, led by a steep drop in postgraduate numbers. NRI Pulse, reporting the Open Doors 2026 release, put the total number of Indian students at 339,435, down 6 percent, with graduate enrolment down 34 percent to 116,609 and participation in Optional Practical Training up 27 percent to 182,201. Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents' Alliance, said the harmful consequences of the administration's policy actions were "already evident in the significant declines in international student enrollment and interest we are witnessing," and that the rule, if implemented, "would have further weakened our ability to attract international talent, disrupted educational plans, and burdened campuses."
